apply_formula.description: Run one formula over a whole list of numbers and get a list of answers back, in the same order. This is the step for a column of figures: add VAT to every price, convert every reading, round every total. Write the formula once using x for each value. It is worked out in a single request however long the list, so it costs the same as one calculation. Every value has to be a number - one that is not stops the step and says which, because Math.js works the list out in one go and cannot skip an entry. No API key required.
apply_formula.display_name: Apply a formula to a list of values
apply_formula.display_str_template: Work out {1} for every value in {0}.
apply_formula.name: apply_formula

parameters.description: The numbers to run the formula over. Wire in a list from an earlier step, or type them one at a time.
parameters.name: values

parameters.description: The formula to apply, written once, with x standing for each value in turn - x * 1.2 adds 20%.
parameters.name: formula

parameters.description: Optional. How many significant digits the answer is worked out to. The default of 14 hides the tiny rounding errors computers make, so 0.1 + 0.2 comes back as 0.3 rather than 0.30000000000000004. Raise it for scientific work that needs the full figure, or lower it for a rough number. This is significant digits, not decimal places - to round to two decimals, use round(value, 2) in the calculation itself.
parameters.name: precision

answers.description: The same answers as text, which is what to use when they carry units.

count.description: How many values were worked out.

precision.description: The significant digits the answers were worked out to.

results.description: One row per value, in the order they were given: the value that went in and the answer that came out.

answer.description: The answer, ready to put in a message. Text answers have the quotation marks Math.js prints around them taken off, and a compound unit is closed up ("62.14 mi/h", not "62.14 mi / h").

input.description: The value the formula was applied to.

items.description: The entries, when the answer is a list or a matrix - numbers where they are numbers. Empty for every other kind of answer.

type.description: What kind of answer this is, and therefore which of the fields beside it to read: "number" (read value), "measurement" (a number with a unit - read value and unit), "list" (read items), "text", "boolean" (the answer is "true" or "false"), "expression" (something algebraic that Math.js could not reduce to a value, such as 5 * x or the complex number 3 + 2i) or "nothing".

unit.description: The unit the answer is in, such as "inch" or "kg", or empty when it has none.

value.description: The answer as a number you can add up, compare or chart - the amount on its own when the answer carries a unit. Empty when the answer is not a number at all, and for Infinity and NaN, which have no numeric form a workflow can carry; the answer field has the word in those two cases.

values.description: Just the answers, as numbers, in the same order as the values that went in. This is the field to wire into another step that wants a list of numbers.

convert_base.description: Take a whole number and get it in all four bases at once - decimal, binary, octal and hexadecimal - each with and without its 0b/0o/0x prefix, so it drops straight into code or into a message. A number pasted in with a prefix is read as that base whatever the field says, so 0xFF works without changing anything. Hexadecimal comes back in upper case, the way it is written. No API key required.
convert_base.name: convert_base

parameters.description: The whole number to convert. Digit separators - spaces, commas or underscores - are ignored, so 1_0110_0111 is fine.
parameters.name: value

parameters.description: Optional. Which base the number is written in. Decimal unless you say otherwise - and a 0b, 0o or 0x prefix on the number itself wins over this.
parameters.name: from_base

binary_digits.description: The binary digits without the prefix ("11111111").

hexadecimal.description: The number in base 16, prefixed and upper case ("0xFF").

hexadecimal_digits.description: The hexadecimal digits without the prefix ("FF") - the form a colour code or a byte is written in.

octal_digits.description: The octal digits without the prefix ("377").

read_as.description: Which base the number was read as: decimal, binary, octal or hexadecimal. Worth checking when a prefix overrode the field.

value.description: The number itself, as a number you can calculate with.

convert_units.description: Convert an amount from one unit into another - kilograms to pounds, Celsius to Fahrenheit, gigabytes to mebibytes, kilometres per hour to miles per hour. Pick both units from the list; there is no syntax to get right, and two units that measure different things are refused before the request rather than coming back as an error. Temperatures are converted properly, offset and all, so 20 Celsius is 68 Fahrenheit rather than 36. The answer comes back as a number and as a sentence you can paste into a message. No API key required.
convert_units.name: convert_units

parameters.description: The unit to convert it into. It has to measure the same kind of thing - a length into a length, a mass into a mass.
parameters.name: to_unit

parameters.description: Optional. How many significant digits the answer is worked out to. The default of 14 hides the tiny rounding errors computers make, so 0.1 + 0.2 comes back as 0.3 rather than 0.30000000000000004. Raise it for scientific work that needs the full figure, or lower it for a rough number. This is significant digits, not decimal places - to round to two decimals, use round(value, 2) in the calculation itself.
parameters.name: precision

differentiate_formula.description: Work out the derivative of a formula with respect to one of its variables - the rate at which it changes. x^2 + 2x differentiated by x is 2 * (x + 1). The answer is simplified on the way out, and any other letters in the formula are held constant. To then get a number from it, put the answer into Evaluate a calculation with the variable as a named value. No API key required.

parameters.description: The formula to differentiate, on one line.
parameters.name: formula

parameters.description: Optional. Which variable to differentiate by. x unless you say otherwise. Every other letter in the formula is treated as a constant.
parameters.name: variable

formula.description: The formula that was given, as it was written.

variable.description: The variable it was differentiated by.

evaluate.description: Work out a calculation and get the answer back as a real number, not text. Write one step per line, exactly as you would on paper: a value you name on one line is there on the next, and the last line is the answer. Handles the things a workflow usually cannot - units (5.08 cm in inch), percentages, trigonometry, matrices, fractions and very large or very precise numbers. Values from earlier steps go in the named values field rather than into the text, so an empty one is reported rather than quietly breaking the sum. No API key required.
evaluate.name: evaluate

parameters.description: What to work out, one step per line. The last line is the answer, and every line's own answer comes back too. Anything after a # is a note to yourself.
parameters.name: expression

parameters.description: Optional. Values from earlier steps, given names the calculation can use - price 19.99, quantity 3. This is the safe way to bring a value in: pasted into the text instead, an empty value breaks the calculation and a negative one silently turns into a subtraction.

get_statistics.description: Summarise a column of numbers in one step: how many there are, their total, smallest, largest and range, the mean, median and most common value, the standard deviation and variance, and the quartiles. Everything is worked out in a single request, so the whole summary costs what one average would. Both the sample and the population standard deviation come back, because which one is meant is the quietest way a figure like this goes wrong. No API key required.
get_statistics.display_name: Get statistics for a list of numbers

mock_response.summary: 6 numbers, from 2 to 9. Mean 5.3333333333333, median 5.5, standard deviation 2.7325202042559.

get_statistics.name: get_statistics

parameters.description: The numbers to summarise. Wire in a list from an earlier step, or type them one at a time.
parameters.name: values

parameters.description: Optional. How many significant digits the answer is worked out to. The default of 14 hides the tiny rounding errors computers make, so 0.1 + 0.2 comes back as 0.3 rather than 0.30000000000000004. Raise it for scientific work that needs the full figure, or lower it for a rough number. This is significant digits, not decimal places - to round to two decimals, use round(value, 2) in the calculation itself.
parameters.name: precision

interquartile_range.description: The distance between the quartiles - the spread of the middle half, ignoring outliers.

lower_quartile.description: The value a quarter of the way through, in order.

mean.description: The average - the total divided by the count.

median.description: The middle value once they are in order. Worth preferring to the mean when a few extreme values would drag it.

mode.description: The most common value. It is a list because several values can tie - and when every number appears once, every number is listed, which is the honest answer that there is no mode.

population_standard_deviation.description: The same spread, treating these numbers as the whole population rather than a sample of one. Slightly smaller, and the right one when the list is genuinely everything.

precision.description: The significant digits the figures were worked out to.

range.description: The distance from smallest to largest.

standard_deviation.description: How spread out they are, treating them as a sample of something larger. This is what a spreadsheet's STDEV gives.

summary.description: The headline figures as a sentence, ready to put in a message.

upper_quartile.description: The value three quarters of the way through.

values.description: The numbers as they were read, in the order given.

variance.description: The sample variance - the standard deviation squared.

simplify_formula.description: Reduce a formula to its simplest equivalent form without working out a number: 2x + 3x becomes 5 * x, and x * 0 + 1 becomes 1. Use it to tidy a formula somebody has typed before showing it back to them, or to collapse one a workflow has built up piece by piece. It says whether anything actually changed. No API key required.
simplify_formula.name: simplify_formula

parameters.description: The formula to simplify, on one line. It can hold any letters you like as variables.
parameters.name: formula

changed.description: Whether simplifying made any difference. False means the formula was already as simple as it gets.

formula.description: The formula that was given, as it was written.

simplified.description: The simplest equivalent form Math.js could find.

description: Do the maths a workflow cannot: work out any calculation and get a real number back, convert units, summarise a column of figures, apply one formula to a whole list, re-base a number, and simplify or differentiate a formula. Math.js is the calculation engine behind mathjs.org, and its web service is free and needs no account or API key.
